title: The dhadis
hook: ballad-singers with small drums and a fiddle sing the panth's history

segments.voice: Yesterday, raga or popular tune: two ways to sing one hymn. Your line was both are loved. When you met two ways of doing one good thing, what did each protect? Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

Halfway through the song, the singer stops singing and starts talking. A Guru on the move, a martyr who wouldn't bend, a battle at a river: the story comes out plainly, and the crowd leans in. Then the drum comes back, a small hourglass drum held up in one hand and struck with the other, with a bowed fiddle crying along beside it, and the story turns into song again. The singers stand rather than sit, and their voices are built to carry across a crowded courtyard. These ballad-singers are today's word.
screen: `AN HOURGLASS DRUM. A FIDDLE.` → `THE SONG STOPS; THE STORY STARTS.` → `THEN THE DRUM AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the name. A dhadi is a ballad-singer who plays the dhad, that small hourglass drum, usually with a sarangi, the bowed fiddle, beside it. Second, a name a Guru took for himself. In a var in Raag Majh, Guru Nanak calls himself a dhadi. In paraphrase: I was a minstrel with no work, and the Lord put me to work, singing praise day and night. Think about that choice. Not a king, not a judge, not a scholar. A wandering ballad-singer, glad to be hired. A humble trade became a Guru's picture of his own calling. Third, history sung. Tradition says Guru Hargobind welcomed dhadis to sing vars, ballads of courage, at the Akal Takht, the seat he raised facing the Harmandir. A var praises those who stood firm. So dhadis turned the panth's story into song: the Gurus, the martyrs, the battles, the families who paid a price. For anyone without a history book, the dhadi was one, out loud, with a drum. Fourth, the way it's done. Song and speech take turns. The singers give a verse; one of them steps out and tells the story plainly; the verse returns, and the crowd now knows why it matters. Dhadi jathas still sing at gurdwaras and gatherings, especially on days that remember martyrs. And this week has been a walk of its own: Baba Bakala, where the Guru was found; Kiratpur's ashes to the river; Hemkunt's high lake; gurdwaras abroad; the rababis; two ways to sing; and now the drum that carries the history.
screen: `DHADI: THE HOURGLASS-DRUM SINGER.` · `GURU NANAK: I WAS A MINSTREL.` · `BALLADS OF COURAGE.` · `SONG, STORY, SONG.` · then, large: `HISTORY SUNG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a dhadi ballad. Settle, and breathe. If you can, find a recording of a dhadi jatha and let a few minutes play: the drum, the fiddle, the voices, the spoken story between. If you can't right now, recall one story from your own family that has been told so often it almost sounds like a song. Hear who first told it. Breathe in on the beat. Breathe out on the story. The bell holds the time.
Dhadi. A ballad-singer with the small hourglass drum, who sings the panth's history; a word Guru Nanak used for himself. Today's word.
Your line: history sung. Today, tell one story from your family's past out loud to someone who hasn't heard it, and let it have a little music in it. Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Dhadi jathas sing vars and ballads of Sikh history with the dhad and sarangi at gurdwaras and gatherings, mixing sung verse with spoken narration, especially on days that remember martyrs.

notes: Guru Nanak's line 'hau dhaadhee vekaar kaarai laaiaa' paraphrased as 'I was a minstrel with no work, and the Lord put me to work, singing praise day and night'. Ang 150 (Majh ki Var) is from memory; please confirm the Ang and the 'day and night' phrasing.
Guru Hargobind's welcome of dhadis at the Akal Takht is given as 'tradition says'; the Akal Takht described as 'the seat he raised facing the Harmandir'. Please confirm.
Dhad as an hourglass drum and sarangi as bowed fiddle; 'singers stand rather than sit' is a general description of performance; please confirm.
